title: TRIA Program Reauthorization Act of 2026
official_title: To extend the Terrorism Risk Insurance Program, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Mike Flood (R-NE) and passed the House 373-15 on June 29, 2026; the bill extends the Terrorism Risk Insurance Program sunset from 2027 to 2034 and revises its certification process, and now awaits Senate consideration.
summary: Extends the federal Terrorism Risk Insurance Program, which is set to end after 2027, so that it now runs through 2034. It also changes how the government decides whether an event counts as an "act of terrorism" for the program, including raising a dollar figure in that definition and adding public-notice steps.
brief: Extends the Terrorism Risk Insurance Program through 2034 and revises how acts of terrorism are certified under it.

top_lines.headline: Program Extension
subs: Extends the Terrorism Risk Insurance Program's sunset from 2027 to 2034
Amends Section 108(a) of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act of 2002

top_lines.headline: Certification Process Changes
subs: Raises a dollar figure in the certification definition from $5M to $25M
Adds a lapse trigger if no certification within 90 days of a Federal Register notice
Requires a Federal Register notice within 30 days of starting a certification review

top_lines.headline: Technical Amendments
subs: Updates statutory year references in Section 103(e)(7)(E)(i)
Renames "Terrorism Insurance Program" to "Terrorism Risk Insurance Program" throughout

items.main: Names the Act the "TRIA Program Reauthorization Act of 2026".
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Amends Section 108(a) of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act of 2002 (15 U.S.C. 6701 note) by striking "2027" and inserting "2034", extending the program's end date.
items.detail: The change moves the sunset year in Section 108(a) from 2027 to 2034. The bill text states only the year substitution; the program's operating terms are set in the underlying Act, which is not reproduced in this bill.

items.main: Amends Section 102(1) of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act of 2002 to raise a dollar figure in the certification definition from $5M to $25M and to add a new condition tied to a 90-day certification window.
items.detail: In subparagraph (B), the bill strikes "$5M" and inserts "$25M", and adds a new clause (iii) providing that the definition is affected if the Secretary did not certify an act as an act of terrorism before the end of the 90-day period following a Federal Register notice under subparagraph (D)(i).

items.main: Replaces subparagraph (D) with new notice requirements directing the Secretary to publish Federal Register notices about the certification process.
items.detail: The Secretary must publish a Federal Register notice, not later than 30 days after beginning the process of determining whether to certify an act as an act of terrorism, informing the public that this determination is underway. The Secretary may also notify the public, through the Federal Register or otherwise, that an act is not being evaluated for certification.

items.main: Updates year references in Section 103(e)(7)(E)(i) of the Act and standardizes the program's name throughout the statute.
items.detail: In subclause (I), "2022" becomes "2029" and "2024" becomes "2031"; in subclause (II), "2023" becomes "2030", "2029" becomes "2036", and "2024" becomes "2031"; in subclause (III), "2029" becomes "2036" and "2024" becomes "2031". Separately, the Act is amended by striking "Terrorism Insurance Program" each place it appears and inserting "Terrorism Risk Insurance Program".

underreported.summary: Adds a condition to the certification definition tied to the Secretary not certifying an act within the 90-day period following a Federal Register notice under subparagraph (D)(i).
underreported.why_unreported: The section is captioned "Improvements to Certification Process," but beyond the threshold change it inserts a time-based condition into the definition itself, keyed to the new 90-day notice window rather than to the certification decision alone.

criticisms.why: Too often, Congress reflexively renews sprawling federal backstops that the market no longer needs--quietly gambling with taxpayers' exposure to potentially massive losses while ignoring the absence of any real market breakdown. This TRIA reauthorization fits the pattern perfectly: another automatic green light for an open-ended federal guarantee, despite no evidence of a genuine market failure.

gaps: The bill raises a dollar figure in the certification definition from $5M to $25M but the bill text does not state the program's other operating parameters it is extending, so a reader cannot see from this text what the program does when triggered.
The bill adds a 90-day certification window and Federal Register notice steps but does not state a consequence within the bill text for the Secretary missing the 30-day or 90-day deadlines.
Section 5 renames "Terrorism Insurance Program" to "Terrorism Risk Insurance Program" throughout but the bill text does not address whether references in other statutes or regulations are conformed.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Flood
featured_quotes.text: I will start today by thanking Chairman Hill, Ranking Member Waters, and my co-lead on this bill, Congressman Andrew Garbarino. All of us have worked together on legislative text that would reauthorize the Terrorism Risk Insurance Program while also making changes that will protect taxpayers. This legislation would reauthorize TRIA, the program established by Congress in the aftermath of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, through 2034. We are so fortunate that we have never seen a TRIA claim in the program's entire history.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Cleaver
featured_quotes.text: I would like to enter into a colloquy with the chairman. I was appalled by reports that a FEMA employee used their authority entrusted by the United States to determine access to Federal aid based on a political yard sign. Whether we are talking about FEMA or the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, this type of action violates the mission of Federal programs that Congress designs to work for all Americans. Likewise, H.R. 7128 is also designed to avoid anything like that from happening in the future with regard to the Terrorism Risk Insurance Program.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Hill
featured_quotes.text: I appreciate the gentleman yielding, and I agree with his assessment. It is true that TRIA was designed to create certainty, not doubt, for our businesses, indeed our economy at large after something unthinkable takes place. It requires insurance companies to make stand-alone terrorism coverage available to their clients, who can choose to purchase it or not in addition to their traditional business insurance coverage.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Rose
featured_quotes.text: Too often Congress reflexively renews sprawling federal backstops that the market no longer needs--quietly gambling with taxpayers' exposure to potentially massive losses while ignoring the absence of any real market breakdown. This TRIA reauthorization fits the pattern perfectly: another automatic green light for an open-ended federal guarantee, despite no evidence of a genuine market failure.

added: New clause (iii) in Section 102(1)(B) tying the certification definition to a 90-day period following a Federal Register notice
New Federal Register notice requirement: the Secretary must publish notice within 30 days of beginning a certification determination
modified: Program name standardized: "Terrorism Insurance Program" → "Terrorism Risk Insurance Program" throughout the Act
removed: Prior subparagraph (D) of Section 102(1), struck and replaced with the new notice requirements

votes.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass
